questions.label: (a)
questions.statement: Define spatial resolution. State what the point spread function (PSF) represents and write the image-formation relationship for a linear, shift-invariant system.
questions.solution: Spatial resolution is the minimum separation at which distinct small features can be resolved. The PSF h is the image of an ideal point object. For a linear, shift-invariant system, I(x,y)=O(x,y)*h(x,y), with * denoting convolution. A finite-width PSF spreads object signal over neighbouring positions.

The PSF h is the image of an ideal point object.
For a linear, shift-invariant system, I(x,y)=O(x,y)*h(x,y), with * denoting convolution.
A finite-width PSF spreads object signal over neighbouring positions.
hints: Use the lecture/source reference: S1 pp.39,45-48.
One proposed marking criterion is: Resolution definition.

questions.label: (c)

questions.solution: An ideal point becomes the Gaussian PSF (scaled by its point strength). The rectangle has rounded edges, nonzero tails and a reduced peak when it is narrow relative to the PSF. Convolution preserves integrated signal for a unit-area PSF, but spreads it; closely spaced fine features can merge.

questions.solution: Choose a physical half-life long enough for distribution and acquisition but short enough to limit unnecessary exposure; predominantly monoenergetic gamma emission with little unnecessary particulate dose; gamma energy suitable for tissue escape and collimator/detector performance (the lecture suggests roughly 100-200 keV); and high target uptake with low background uptake to improve contrast.

questions.label: (e)
questions.statement: Using a labeled sketch, explain positron annihilation coincidence detection in PET. Give two benefits of combining PET with CT.
questions.solution: The tracer emits a positron which slows in tissue and annihilates with an electron. The dominant two-photon event produces two approximately opposite 511 keV photons. Opposing detector signals accepted within a coincidence time window define a line of response (LOR), rather than an exact point. Many LORs reconstruct tracer distribution. CT supplies anatomical localization and an attenuation map for PET correction.

Many LORs reconstruct tracer distribution.
CT supplies anatomical localization and an attenuation map for PET correction.

questions.label: (f)
questions.statement: A 2×2 image has unit-weight ray sums: top row 6, bottom row 10, left column 7 and right column 9. Start all pixels at zero. Perform one ART sweep in that order, adding each ray residual equally to its two pixels. Report every intermediate image and determine whether these data uniquely identify all four pixels.

The common ρ·exp(-TE/T2*) factor cancels.
With the same noise, SNR loss=100(1-0.79506010)=20.49399%, approximately 20.5%.

questions.label: (f)
questions.statement: Explain why a conventional spin echo is less sensitive than GE to static magnetic-field inhomogeneity. Sketch the RF and signal timing and state which transverse relaxation time governs the ideal echo envelope.
questions.solution: A 90° excitation creates transverse magnetization; static field offsets make spins accumulate different phases. A 180° RF pulse at TE/2 reverses their relative phase positions. Stationary spins with constant offsets rephase at TE, producing an echo. Intrinsic irreversible T2 decay is not recovered. The ideal spin-echo envelope is exp(-TE/T2); gradient echo alone does not reverse static field-offset dephasing and retains T2* effects.

A 180° RF pulse at TE/2 reverses their relative phase positions.
Stationary spins with constant offsets rephase at TE, producing an echo.
Intrinsic irreversible T2 decay is not recovered.
The ideal spin-echo envelope is exp(-TE/T2); gradient echo alone does not reverse static field-offset dephasing and retains T2* effects.

Gel replaces the air gap with an acoustic coupling layer and improves transmission.

The true structures remain aligned while speckle is partly decorrelated. Repeating an identical view does not give the same improvement as averaging independent electronic noise.

questions.label: (e)
questions.statement: Describe the physical cause and image appearance of (i) reverberation and (ii) posterior acoustic enhancement.
questions.solution: Reverberation occurs when a pulse reflects repeatedly between strong interfaces (often probe and a nearby strong reflector). Longer travel paths are mapped as deeper echoes, producing repeated, often equally spaced lines. Enhancement occurs behind a region that attenuates less than the surrounding tissue, such as a fluid-filled region; deeper echoes are brighter than expected under the same gain compensation.

questions.label: (f)
questions.statement: Draw a basic time-domain OCT interferometer. Explain depth selection and the formation of A- and B-scans. State one medical application and one limitation.
questions.solution: A broadband, low-temporal-coherence light source is split into sample and reference arms. Returning sample backscatter and reference-mirror light recombine at a detector. Significant interference envelope occurs when their optical path lengths match within the coherence length. Moving the reference mirror samples optical delay and gives a depth reflectivity profile (A-scan); lateral translation yields successive A-scans forming a cross-sectional B-scan. Retinal-layer imaging is an application. Tissue scattering/absorption limits penetration, so OCT is best for transparent or superficial structures.

questions.statement: A real low-pass analogue signal contains frequencies up to 18 kHz. State the theoretical Nyquist sampling bound and explain the role of an analogue anti-alias filter. It assumes adequately uncorrelated/noise-like quantization errors; oversampling alone cannot guarantee extra bits for a deterministic undithered error.

Most tube electron energy becomes heat.

questions.statement: Compare photoelectric absorption and Compton scattering for diagnostic X-rays. Explain why pair production is not significant at a maximum tube photon energy of 120 keV.
questions.solution: Photoelectric absorption removes the incident photon and ejects a bound electron; its strong dependence on photon energy and effective atomic number contributes to tissue/contrast-agent differences. Pair production requires at least approximately 1.022 MeV, well above 120 keV=0.120 MeV, so it is energetically impossible for that beam.

questions.statement: State suitable qualitative TR and TE choices for proton-density-weighted, T1-weighted and T2-weighted conventional spin-echo images. Explain why long TR reduces T1 contrast.

questions.statement: Explain the BOLD basis of fMRI, why rapid EPI acquisition is useful, and how a simple repeated task/rest experiment identifies associated regions. State one interpretation limitation.

questions.solution: The large acoustic-impedance mismatch causes strong reflection and poor transmission through the interface.
